why.correct: The belly is the thick, fleshy middle of a muscle, between the tendons that run to its origin and insertion.
options: The origin is the attachment that stays still, at one end of the muscle, not its fleshy middle.
Correct. The fleshy middle part of the muscle is its belly.
The insertion is the attachment on the bone that moves, at the other end of the muscle.
An aponeurosis is a flat sheet of dense connective tissue that attaches some muscles. It is not the fleshy middle.

why.correct: Fascicles that attach at an angle on both sides of one central tendon, like both sides of a feather, make a bipennate muscle.
options: A unipennate muscle has fascicles on only one side of its tendon.
A multipennate muscle has several tendons, with fascicles converging on them from many angles.
Correct. Fascicles on both sides of a central tendon are bipennate.
A convergent muscle fans out from one tendon over a broad origin. Its fascicles do not line both sides of a long central tendon.

why.correct: A fan of fascicles spreading from one tendon over a broad origin is a convergent arrangement.
options: Parallel fascicles run side by side along the whole length of the muscle, not in a fan.
Correct. A fan-shaped muscle whose fascicles meet at one tendon is convergent.
Circular fascicles run in rings around an opening, as around the mouth.
Unipennate fascicles slant into one side of a long tendon, like half a feather.

why.correct: Fascicles running in a ring around an opening form a circular muscle. One that guards an opening is called a sphincter.
options: Convergent fascicles fan out from one tendon; they do not form a ring.
Multipennate fascicles slant onto several tendons, as in the thick muscle over the shoulder.
A fusiform muscle is a parallel muscle with a thick belly tapering at both ends.
Correct. The ring of fascicles around the mouth is a circular muscle.

why.correct: The insertion is the attachment on the bone that moves. When you lift the cup, the forearm (with the radius) swings up while the scapula stays put, so the radius attachment is the insertion and the scapula attachment is the origin.
options: The scapula stays still while the forearm moves, which makes the scapula attachment the origin. Being higher does not decide it.
The origin is the stable attachment. The radius moves when you lift the cup, so its attachment is the insertion.
A muscle has an origin at the stable end and an insertion at the moving end, not two origins. (Some muscles have several heads at their origin, but they still have an insertion.)
Correct. The radius moves, so that attachment is the insertion.

why.correct: With the hands fixed on the ledge, the forearm is the stable end. The muscles still pull their two ends together, but now the upper arm and trunk (the usual origin) move up toward the forearm (the usual insertion). This is a reverse action.
options: Muscles only pull; they cannot push bones apart.
Correct. The usual origin moves toward the fixed insertion.
In a pull-up the forearm is fixed, so the insertion is not the part that moves.
Bending the elbow is still flexion, so the flexors on the front of the arm remain the prime movers. The muscles on the back of the arm straighten the elbow.

why.correct: The prime mover (agonist) does most of the work, synergists help or steady it, fixators hold the base still, and the antagonist makes the opposite movement. Roles belong to movements: the same muscle can be an antagonist in one movement and the prime mover in the next.
options: Correct. Prime mover and agonist are two names for the muscle most responsible for a movement.
Correct. Synergists add force to the same movement or keep it moving in the right direction.
Correct. A fixator is a kind of synergist that stabilizes the bone the prime mover pulls from.
Incorrect. An antagonist makes the opposite movement; it relaxes and lengthens, often braking, while the prime mover contracts.
Incorrect. The muscle on the back of the arm is the antagonist when you bend the elbow and the prime mover when you straighten it.

why.correct: Muscles that hold a bone still so other muscles can pull from it are fixators. With a loose scapula, the arm muscles have no steady base, so their pull moves the scapula instead of the arm.
options: Correct. Holding the scapula steady as a base is the fixator's job.
Antagonists produce the opposite movement. Weak antagonists would not make the scapula slide during a push.
The elbow's prime movers straighten or bend the elbow. They work from the arm bones, not from the scapula's position on the rib cage.
A sphincter is a ring of muscle that closes an opening, such as the mouth. It plays no part in pushing a door.

why.correct: The joint (fulcrum) sits between the effort at the back of the skull and the load of the face in front. A fulcrum in the middle makes a first-class lever, like a seesaw.
options: In a second-class lever the load sits in the middle, between the fulcrum and the effort. Here the joint is in the middle.
In a third-class lever the effort sits in the middle. Here the muscles pull behind the joint, not between the joint and the face.
Correct. Fulcrum in the middle makes a first-class lever.
The skull is a rigid bar turning about a joint under a muscle's pull, which is exactly what a lever is.

why.correct: Rising onto the toes is the standard second-class example: the ball of the foot is the fulcrum, body weight is the load in the middle, and the calf muscles pull up on the heel bone at the far end.
options: Bending the elbow is third-class: the muscle's pull lies between the elbow and the load in the hand.
Correct. The load sits between the fulcrum at the ball of the foot and the effort at the heel.
Closing the jaw is third-class: the chewing muscles pull between the jaw joint and the food.
Nodding at the atlanto-occipital joint is first-class: the joint lies between the effort and the load.

why.correct: The muscles pull between the fulcrum (the jaw joint) and the load (the nut at the front teeth). Effort in the middle makes a third-class lever.
options: A first-class lever has the fulcrum in the middle. Here the jaw joint is at one end.
A second-class lever has the load in the middle. Here the nut is at the far end.
Correct. Effort in the middle is third-class.
Each lever has one arrangement; with the effort in the middle, this one is simply third-class.

why.correct: At balance, effort × effort arm = load × load arm. Effort × 5 cm = 20 N × 30 cm = 600 N·cm, so effort = 600 ÷ 5 = 120 N. The muscle pulls six times the load, because its effort arm is one sixth as long as the load arm.
options: About 3 N would come from dividing the load by the six-fold ratio. With the effort arm shorter than the load arm, the muscle must pull more than the load, not less.
Pulling with the same force as the load would balance only if both arms were the same length.
Correct. 20 N × 30 cm ÷ 5 cm = 120 N.
600 is the product of the load and its arm (600 N·cm). It still has to be divided by the 5-cm effort arm.

why.correct: With the effort arm shorter than the load arm, a short shortening of the muscle swings the far end of the bone a long way in the same time, so the hand or foot moves far and fast. The price is a mechanical advantage below 1: the muscle and tendon carry forces several times the load.
options: A third-class lever loses force, not gains it: its effort arm is always shorter than its load arm.
Correct. Range and speed are gained; force is lost.
The lever class does not set joint stability or the planes a joint moves in; the joint's shape and ligaments do.
The arrangement has a clear mechanical effect: it multiplies the distance and speed of movement at the end of the limb.

why.correct: Short, angled fibers let more fibers pack side by side into the pennate muscle, so more cross-bridges pull at once and it is stronger. Long parallel fibers have more sarcomeres in series, so the parallel muscle shortens a longer distance, faster.
options: Correct. Pennate means more force; parallel means more range and speed.
This reverses both effects. More fibers side by side gives the pennate muscle more force; longer fibers give the parallel muscle more range.
Force depends on how many fibers pull side by side, not on volume alone. The pennate muscle fits more fibers into the same volume.
Short fibers cannot shorten as far as long ones. The pennate muscle gives up range to gain force.

why.correct: The signal makes the fibers shorten. Their pull passes through the wrappings into the tendon, which pulls the insertion toward the origin. The forearm turns about the elbow as a lever, and because the insertion is close to the elbow, the hand travels much farther than the insertion does.
options: The movement starts with the motor neurons firing the muscle's fibers.
Shortening fibers pull on the endomysium, perimysium and epimysium around them.
The wrappings merge into the tendon, which transmits the pull to the insertion.
Pulled at its insertion, the forearm turns about the elbow joint.
With the effort close to the fulcrum, the far end of the lever moves farther and faster.

why.correct: Pollex is Latin for thumb, and pollicis means "of the thumb". Flexor pollicis longus is the long muscle that flexes the thumb.
options: Correct. Pollicis means of the thumb.
The smallest finger is digiti minimi, as in abductor digiti minimi.
The chest is pectoral-.
Two heads is biceps (-ceps = heads).

why.correct: In an ordinary curl the scapula is held still and the forearm moves, so the insertion moves toward the origin, not the other way round.
options: Correct statement. The front upper-arm muscle is the prime mover for elbow flexion.
Correct statement. Muscles beneath it and in the forearm are synergists for flexion.
Correct statement. Fixators steady the scapula so the prime mover has a stable base.
This is the wrong one. The scapula (origin) stays still; the forearm (insertion) moves toward it.
Correct statement. The antagonist lengthens while the prime mover contracts.

why.correct: Moving the insertion away from the joint lengthens the effort arm. The lever gains mechanical advantage, so less muscle force is needed, but it loses the multiplication of distance and speed at the hand.

variables.name: Mechanical advantage (effort arm ÷ load arm)
variables.why: The effort arm doubles while the load arm stays the same, so the ratio doubles.

variables.name: Force the muscle must pull with to hold the weight
variables.why: Effort × effort arm must equal load × load arm. With a longer effort arm, a smaller effort balances the same load.

variables.name: Distance the hand moves for each centimeter the muscle shortens
variables.why: The ratio of load arm to effort arm falls, so each centimeter of shortening swings the hand through a shorter distance: force is gained, range and speed are lost.

why.correct: Gravity would drop the bag. The front upper-arm muscle keeps its cross-bridges working while it is pulled longer, an eccentric contraction, so it controls the speed of the fall.
options: Correct. This is an eccentric contraction that brakes the movement.
If it relaxed completely, the bag would drop. In slow lowering, gravity straightens the elbow, not the antagonist, and the flexor controls the rate.
Muscles cannot push; they can only pull.
The front muscle bends the elbow when it shortens. Here the elbow is straightening, so it is lengthening.

why.correct: Rectus means straight. It names a muscle by the direction of its fascicles, which run parallel to the body's midline or to the long axis of a bone.
options: Correct. Rectus describes straight fascicles.
Largest is maximus.
A muscle that closes an opening is a sphincter; orbicularis (small circle) describes its ring shape.
Three heads is triceps.

why.correct: The fulcrum is the fixed pivot a lever turns about. In the body, the bone is the bar and the joint is the fulcrum.
options: Where the muscle pulls is the effort, not the fulcrum.
Correct. The joint is the fulcrum.
The weight being moved is the load.
The belly is the fleshy middle of a muscle. It is part of the effort side, not a pivot.

why.correct: The ring of muscle around the eye is the orbicularis oculi. It closes the eyelids.
options: The orbicularis oris is the ring around the mouth, not the eye.
Correct. The ring around the eye is the orbicularis oculi.
The frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis lies over the forehead, above the eye; it raises the eyebrows rather than closing the eye.
The temporalis is a chewing muscle on the side of the skull, under the scalp, not around the eye.

why.correct: The buccinator forms the wall of the cheek, running from the maxilla and mandible beside the molars forward into the corner of the mouth.
options: The masseter lies farther back, over the angle of the mandible, and moves the jaw rather than the cheek.
The zygomaticus major runs diagonally from the cheekbone down to the corner of the mouth, above the cheek wall.
Correct. The flat muscle of the cheek wall is the buccinator.
The orbicularis oris is the ring around the lips, which the buccinator runs into.

why.correct: The epicranial aponeurosis is the flat sheet of tendon over the top of the skull that joins the frontal and occipital bellies of the occipitofrontalis.
options: Correct. The tendon sheet between the two bellies of the scalp muscle is the epicranial aponeurosis.
The occipital belly is the muscle at the back of the skull that inserts on this sheet, not the sheet itself.
The facial muscles have no deep fascia over them. The scalp sheet is an aponeurosis, a flat tendon.
The temporalis lies on the side of the skull, below this sheet.

why.correct: The masseter runs from the zygomatic arch down to the outer surface of the angle of the mandible. It is the prime mover of jaw closing.
options: The temporalis fans over the side of the skull above the ear, not over the angle of the jaw.
The buccinator lies forward in the cheek wall and moves the cheek, not the jaw.
The medial pterygoid inserts on the inner surface of the angle of the mandible, hidden from this outside view.
Correct. The thick muscle over the angle of the jaw is the masseter.

why.correct: The temporalis fans across the temporal fossa and converges on a tendon that inserts on the coronoid process of the mandible. It elevates and retracts the jaw.
options: Correct. The fan over the temple is the temporalis.
The occipitalis is at the back of the skull and moves the scalp.
The masseter lies lower, below the zygomatic arch over the angle of the jaw.
The lateral pterygoid lies deep, inside the upright back part of the mandible, and cannot be seen from the side without dissection.

why.correct: The lateral pterygoid runs nearly horizontally from the sphenoid bone back to the condyle of the mandible and the joint's disc. It protracts the jaw and helps open the mouth.
options: The medial pterygoid runs nearly vertically, down to the inner surface of the angle of the mandible.
Correct. The horizontal deep muscle to the condyle is the lateral pterygoid.
The temporalis is superficial on the side of the skull and inserts on the coronoid process.
The masseter is superficial, on the outer surface of the mandible.

why.correct: The sternocleidomastoid runs from the manubrium and medial clavicle up and back to the mastoid process behind the ear.
options: The scalenes lie deeper and lower on the side of the neck, running from the cervical vertebrae to the first two ribs.
The omohyoid is a thin infrahyoid strap muscle running from the scapula to the hyoid.
Correct. The long diagonal muscle from sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process is the sternocleidomastoid.
The digastric is a suprahyoid muscle under the jaw.

why.correct: The scalenes run from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae to the first and second ribs, deep on the side of the neck.
options: The infrahyoid muscles are on the front of the neck below the hyoid, not on the side.
The suprahyoid muscles are under the jaw, above the hyoid.
The sternocleidomastoid is the single large superficial muscle crossing the side of the neck diagonally.
Correct. These are the scalenes.

why.correct: The digastric (di- = two, gaster = belly) has two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon held to the hyoid by a loop.
options: The mylohyoid is a flat sheet forming the floor of the mouth, with one belly.
The sternohyoid is an infrahyoid strap muscle, below the hyoid.
Correct. Two bellies make it the digastric.
The omohyoid also has two bellies, but it is an infrahyoid muscle below the hyoid, running to the scapula.

why.correct: The orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids, so its weakness leaves the eye partly open. The buccinator presses the cheek against the teeth and pushes food back onto them, so its weakness lets food collect in the cheek.
options: The masseter and temporalis close the jaw. Weakness would make biting weak, not keep the eye open or let food pocket in the cheek.
The frontalis raises the eyebrow and the zygomaticus major lifts the corner of the mouth. Neither closes the eye or clears the cheek.
Correct. The eye sphincter and the cheek muscle explain both problems.
The pterygoids move the jaw forward and side to side. They do not close the eye or press the cheek to the teeth.

why.correct: The muscle pulls the mastoid process toward the sternum and clavicle on the same side. That tilts the head toward the right shoulder and, because the mastoid is behind the ear, swings the face toward the left.
options: Correct. Same-side tilt, opposite-side turn.
This describes the left sternocleidomastoid.
Straight neck flexion needs both sternocleidomastoids contracting together.
Tipping the head back is extension, done mainly by muscles at the back of the neck.

why.correct: The masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid all insert on the mandible and pull it up. The lateral pterygoid and the suprahyoid muscles, such as the digastric, help open the jaw instead.
options: Yes. The masseter is the prime mover of jaw closing.
Yes. The temporalis elevates and retracts the mandible.
Yes. The medial pterygoid elevates the mandible from the inside, mirroring the masseter.
No. The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression: it presses the cheek to the teeth but does not move the jaw.
No. The digastric is a suprahyoid muscle; with the hyoid held still it pulls the mandible down, opening the mouth.

why.correct: Most facial expression muscles originate on skull bone and insert into skin, so their pull moves the skin of the face, not a bone.
options: They are skeletal muscles, striated and under voluntary control.
Correct. Their insertion into skin is what lets them change your expression.
They do have origins, usually on skull bones or on the epicranial aponeurosis.
You can smile, frown or raise your eyebrows on purpose; they are voluntary skeletal muscles.

why.correct: The buccinator (the "trumpeter" muscle) forms the cheek wall and presses it inward against the teeth, raising the pressure of air in the mouth.
options: The masseter closes the jaw. It lies over the cheek but does not press the cheek wall in.
The zygomaticus major pulls the corner of the mouth up and back, as in a smile.
The frontalis raises the eyebrows.
Correct. The buccinator compresses the cheek.

why.correct: The suprahyoid muscles run from the hyoid up to the mandible and skull, so they pull it up. The infrahyoid muscles run from the hyoid down to the sternum, voice box and scapula, so they pull it back down.
options: This reverses them. Muscles below the hyoid pull it down, not up.
Correct. Above pulls up, below pulls down.
The scalenes attach to the vertebrae and ribs, and the sternocleidomastoids to the sternum, clavicle and mastoid. Neither attaches to the hyoid.
The masseters attach the zygomatic arch to the mandible and never reach the hyoid; muscles below the hyoid actively pull it down.

why.correct: With the hyoid fixed by the infrahyoid muscles, the suprahyoid muscles' other attachment, on the mandible, becomes the end that moves, so they pull the jaw down.
options: Correct. The suprahyoids depress the mandible when the hyoid is held still.
The masseters close the jaw; they are antagonists of opening.
The scalenes run from the neck vertebrae to the ribs and do not reach the mandible.
The temporalis muscles elevate the mandible, closing the jaw.

why.correct: The sternocleidomastoid inserts on the mastoid process, the bump you can feel behind your ear. Its name says so: stern- (sternum), cleido- (clavicle), mastoid.
options: Correct step. The sternal head comes from the manubrium.
Correct step. The clavicular head comes from the medial clavicle.
Correct step. The heads merge and run diagonally up and back.
This is the wrong step. It inserts on the mastoid process, not the styloid process.

why.correct: The suprahyoids raise the hyoid in swallowing and help open the jaw. Paralysis weakens both of those, but leaves the jaw-closing muscles, and so the bite, unchanged.

variables.name: How high the hyoid rises during a swallow
variables.why: The suprahyoid muscles are what pull the hyoid up toward the mandible, so without them it barely rises.

variables.name: Strength of opening the mouth against a hand under the chin
variables.why: With the hyoid held still, the suprahyoids pull the mandible down. Losing them leaves only the lateral pterygoids and gravity to open the jaw.

variables.name: Biting force of the molars
variables.why: Biting is jaw closing by the masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid, which are unaffected.

why.correct: The lateral pterygoid runs almost horizontally from the sphenoid bone back to the condyle, so its pull draws the condyle, and the whole mandible, forward.
options: The masseter mainly elevates the mandible, closing the jaw.
The temporalis elevates the mandible, and its back fibers retract it, the opposite of protraction.
Correct. The lateral pterygoid protracts the jaw.
The buccinator moves the cheek, not the mandible.

why.correct: The frontalis, the frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis, pulls up on the skin of the eyebrows and forehead from its origin on the epicranial aponeurosis.
options: The orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids, which pulls the brows down rather than up.
Correct. The frontalis raises the eyebrows.
The occipitalis pulls the scalp backward; it anchors the aponeurosis but does not lift the brows by itself.
The temporalis is a chewing muscle; it moves the jaw, not the skin.

why.correct: The masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid are large muscles that all elevate the mandible. Opening uses only the lateral pterygoids and the thin suprahyoid muscles, with gravity helping, so it is far weaker.
options: Lever class does not explain it: opening and closing both turn the mandible about the same jaw joint. The difference is how much muscle pulls each way.
All chewing and neck muscles here are skeletal muscle.
Correct. Much more muscle closes the jaw than opens it.
The joint does not lock open; it slides and hinges freely through both movements.

why.correct: The external oblique is the outermost of the three flat abdominal muscles. It originates on the lower eight ribs, and its fascicles run down and toward the midline.
options: The internal oblique lies just beneath the external oblique, with fibers at right angles to it.
The transversus abdominis is the deepest of the three flat muscles, with horizontal fibers.
Correct. The outermost flat muscle is the external oblique.
The rectus abdominis is the vertical strap at the front, beside the midline, not the flat muscle of the side wall.

why.correct: The transversus abdominis is the innermost flat muscle. Its fibers run horizontally around the belly like a belt, and compressing the abdomen is its main job.
options: Correct. Horizontal fibers in the deepest layer mark the transversus abdominis.
The internal oblique is the middle layer, with fibers running up and toward the midline.
The external oblique is the outermost layer, with fibers running down and toward the midline.
The aponeurosis of the internal oblique is the flat tendon sheet of the middle layer, running toward the midline; it is not the deepest muscle layer.

why.correct: The quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest to the twelfth rib and the lumbar transverse processes, forming part of the back wall of the abdomen.
options: The transversus abdominis wraps the front and sides of the abdomen, not the back wall between rib and pelvis.
The erector spinae lies behind the vertebrae, along the back, not in the abdominal back wall seen from the front.
The rectus abdominis runs up the front of the abdomen.
Correct. This is the quadratus lumborum.

why.correct: The iliocostalis is the outermost (most lateral) of the three columns of the erector spinae, running from the iliac crest to the ribs. In the lower back it is the iliocostalis lumborum.
options: The spinalis is the most medial column, running between the spinous processes.
The longissimus, here the longissimus thoracis, is the middle column.
Correct. The outermost column is the iliocostalis.
The splenius lies at the back of the neck and upper back, not in the lower back.

why.correct: The diaphragm's muscle fibers run from the lower edge of the rib cage and the lumbar vertebrae to its central tendon, which they pull down when they contract.
options: The linea alba is the midline seam of the front abdominal wall, not part of the diaphragm.
Correct. This is the central tendon of the diaphragm.
The epicranial aponeurosis covers the top of the skull.
The rectus sheath wraps the rectus abdominis in the front abdominal wall.

why.correct: The external intercostals form the outer layer between the ribs. Their fibers run down and forward, and they lift the ribs when you breathe in.
options: The internal intercostals lie beneath the externals, with fibers running down and back.
The innermost intercostals are the deepest layer.
Correct. The outer layer with down-and-forward fibers is the external intercostal.
The external oblique covers the abdomen below the ribs; it does not fill the spaces between ribs.

why.correct: The levator ani is the broad funnel of the pelvic floor. Its parts, the pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus, run from the pubis and the side walls of the pelvis to the coccyx.
options: Correct. The two parts together make the levator ani.
The coccygeus is the small triangular muscle behind the levator ani, from the ischial spine to the sacrum and coccyx.
The transversus abdominis wraps the abdomen; it does not form the floor of the pelvis.
The quadratus lumborum is in the back wall of the abdomen, above the pelvis.

why.correct: Beneath the skin and subcutaneous tissue, the three flat muscles lie outermost to innermost: external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis.
options: The skin is the outer covering.
The subcutaneous tissue lies under the skin.
The external oblique is the outermost muscle layer.
The internal oblique lies beneath the external oblique, its fibers at right angles.
The transversus abdominis is the deepest of the three flat muscles.

why.correct: An external oblique turns the trunk toward the opposite side and an internal oblique toward the same side. Turning right uses the left external oblique and the right internal oblique, whose fibers line up diagonally across the body.
options: This pair turns the trunk to the left.
Correct. Left external plus right internal turns the trunk right.
The two external obliques pull in opposite rotational directions, so together they flex the trunk and compress the abdomen rather than turn it.
The rectus abdominis muscles flex the spine; they do not rotate it.

why.correct: The rectus abdominis runs straight up the front of the abdomen from the pubis to the xiphoid process and ribs 5 to 7, and it flexes the spine and compresses the abdomen.
options: Correct. Its origin is the pubic crest and pubic symphysis.
Correct. It inserts on the xiphoid process and the costal cartilages of ribs 5 to 7.
Correct. It is the prime mover of a sit-up or curl.
Incorrect. Rectus means straight: its fibers run vertically. Horizontal fibers belong to the transversus abdominis.
Incorrect. It is in the front wall. The quadratus lumborum is in the back wall.

why.correct: A cough raises the pressure inside the abdomen. The levator ani normally contracts at the same moment, supporting the bladder and squeezing the urethra shut. Stretched or torn during birth, it cannot hold against the pressure, so urine leaks.
options: A weak rectus abdominis would make the cough weaker, lowering the pressure on the bladder rather than letting urine escape.
The diaphragm forms the top of the abdominal cavity. It does not close the urethra.
The quadratus lumborum is in the back wall of the abdomen and does not support the pelvic organs.
Correct. The weakened pelvic floor fails to resist the pressure rise.

why.correct: The diaphragm's fibers run from the lower rim of the rib cage to the central tendon at the top of the dome. Shortening, they pull the tendon down, so the dome flattens and the chest cavity gets taller. Air flows in.
options: Correct. Contraction flattens and lowers the dome.
The dome rises when the diaphragm relaxes, not when it contracts.
Pulling the ribs down is done by the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles, in forceful breathing out.
Contraction enlarges the chest, so air flows in, not out.

why.correct: A forceful breath out is active. The internal intercostals (with the innermost intercostals and the abdominal muscles) pull the ribs down and in, shrinking the chest fast.
options: The external intercostals do lift the ribs, but that enlarges the chest for breathing in.
The external intercostals' down-and-forward fibers lift the ribs, not lower them.
Correct. The internal intercostals lower the ribs in forceful breathing out.
Most of the internal intercostals lower the ribs; lifting them would draw air in.

why.correct: A cough is a sudden squeeze by the abdominal wall. The pressure rise pushes the diaphragm up and air out, while the pelvic floor contracts to hold the bottom of the trunk closed.

variables.name: Pressure inside the abdomen
variables.why: The rectus abdominis, obliques and transversus abdominis squeeze the abdomen, and its soft contents cannot be compressed, so the pressure rises.

variables.name: Height of the diaphragm's dome
variables.why: The pressurized abdominal contents push up on the relaxed diaphragm, driving it higher into the chest and forcing air out.

variables.name: Contraction of the levator ani
variables.why: The pelvic floor contracts with the abdominal wall, holding the pelvic organs up against the pressure rise and keeping the urethra closed.

why.correct: The linea alba (white line) is the collagen seam where the two rectus sheaths meet, from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis.
options: The central tendon is the tendon at the top of the diaphragm.
Correct. The two sheaths meet at the linea alba.
The inguinal ligament is the lower free edge of the external oblique's aponeurosis, in the groin, not the midline seam.
Tendinous intersections cross each rectus abdominis horizontally; they do not join the two sides.

why.correct: Flattening the dome lowers the floor of the chest, so the chest cavity becomes taller, not shorter. A larger chest is what lets air flow in.
options: Correct step. A breath in starts with the diaphragm contracting.
Correct step. The fibers insert on the central tendon and pull it down.
Correct step. With the tendon pulled down, the dome flattens.
This is the wrong step. The chest cavity becomes taller.
Correct step. The enlarged chest lets air flow in.

why.correct: The anal triangle, behind the line between the ischial tuberosities, contains the anal opening.
options: Correct. The anal triangle holds the anal opening.
The urethral opening and the external genitals are in the urogenital triangle, in front.
The pubic symphysis is the front corner of the whole diamond, in the urogenital triangle.
The central tendon belongs to the diaphragm, at the top of the abdomen.

why.correct: Breathing out at rest is passive. The diaphragm and intercostals relax, and the stretched lungs and chest wall spring back, pushing air out.
options: The internal intercostals join in only when you breathe out forcefully.
The abdominal muscles squeeze air out only in forceful breathing out, a cough or a sneeze.
The diaphragm contracts to breathe in; it relaxes as you breathe out.
Correct. Breathing out at rest needs no muscle contraction.

why.correct: One splenius turns the face toward its own side; one sternocleidomastoid turns it toward the opposite side. So a turn to the right pairs the right splenius with the left sternocleidomastoid.
options: The right sternocleidomastoid turns the face to the left, against the movement.
The left splenius turns the face to the left, against the movement.
Correct. Right splenius plus left sternocleidomastoid turn the face right.
The erector spinae mainly extends the spine and bends it to the side; it is not the partner that turns the head.

why.correct: Bands of tendon called tendinous intersections cross each rectus abdominis, dividing it into blocks. The linea alba runs down the middle between the two sides.
options: The flat muscles lie on the sides of the abdomen, not across the front blocks.
Correct. The tendinous intersections create the blocks.
The linea alba is a single vertical seam; it separates right from left, not one block from the next.
The costal cartilages are higher, at the edge of the rib cage, and form no blocks on the abdomen.

why.correct: The diaphragm above, the pelvic floor below and the abdominal wall around all contract, so the abdomen becomes a sealed, pressurized cylinder. Its contents cannot be compressed, so it stiffens the trunk and shares the load on the spine.
options: The erector spinae must work hard during the lift; bracing adds support, it does not let them relax.
Correct. Raised pressure in a sealed abdomen stiffens the trunk.
Tightening the belly raises the pressure in the abdomen, it does not lower it, and the organs' weight is unchanged.
The lungs stay in the chest above the diaphragm; they cannot reach the lumbar spine.

why.correct: The serratus anterior's finger-like slips come from the upper eight or nine ribs and wrap around to the medial border of the scapula.
options: The pectoralis minor runs from ribs 3 to 5 up to the coracoid process; it has no saw-tooth row of slips along the side of the chest.
Correct. The saw-toothed slips on the ribs are the serratus anterior.
The external intercostals fill the spaces between the ribs, beneath these slips; they do not wrap back to the scapula.
The latissimus dorsi covers the lower back and side, behind this muscle.

why.correct: The trapezius runs from the skull and the spine down to T12 and out to the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula. Its parts elevate, retract and depress the scapula.
options: The rhomboids lie under the trapezius, between the spine and the medial border of the scapula.
The latissimus dorsi covers the lower back, below the trapezius.
The deltoid caps the shoulder, lateral to the trapezius.
Correct. The large diamond over the upper back is the trapezius.

why.correct: The latissimus dorsi (widest of the back) runs from the lower spine, sacrum, iliac crest and lowest ribs to the intertubercular groove of the humerus.
options: Correct. The widest muscle of the back is the latissimus dorsi.
The trapezius covers the upper back and neck, above this muscle.
The teres major is a much smaller muscle running from the inferior angle of the scapula to the humerus.
The erector spinae lies deeper, in columns right beside the spine.

why.correct: The infraspinatus fills the infraspinous fossa, below the spine of the scapula, and inserts on the greater tubercle. It rotates the arm laterally.
options: The supraspinatus lies above the spine of the scapula, in the supraspinous fossa.
The teres major runs from the inferior angle of the scapula; it is not part of the rotator cuff.
Correct. Below the spine is the infraspinatus.
The subscapularis lies on the rib-side face of the scapula and cannot be seen from behind.

why.correct: The subscapularis fills the subscapular fossa on the front (rib-side) face of the scapula and inserts on the lesser tubercle. It rotates the arm medially.
options: The serratus anterior runs from the ribs to the medial border of the scapula; its slips lie on the chest wall, not in the scapula's front hollow.
Correct. The rotator cuff muscle on the front of the scapula is the subscapularis.
The pectoralis minor runs from ribs 3 to 5 to the coracoid process, in front of the scapula but not filling its hollow.
The teres minor is on the back, along the lateral border of the scapula.

why.correct: The brachioradialis runs from the lateral edge of the lower humerus to the styloid process of the radius. It flexes the elbow, most strongly with the thumb up.
options: The pronator teres runs diagonally across the upper forearm from the medial epicondyle to the middle of the radius.
The flexor carpi radialis starts on the medial epicondyle and runs to the wrist, closer to the middle of the forearm.
Correct. This is the brachioradialis.
The brachialis lies in the arm under the biceps brachii and ends at the ulna, not in the forearm.

why.correct: The pronator quadratus is a flat four-sided muscle across the lower ends of the ulna and radius. It is the main pronator of the forearm.
options: The supinator wraps the upper radius near the elbow, not the lower end near the wrist.
The pronator teres is a diagonal muscle in the upper forearm, from the medial epicondyle to the middle of the radius.
The flexor digitorum profundus is a long muscle whose tendons run to the fingertips.
Correct. The square muscle near the wrist is the pronator quadratus.

why.correct: The extensor digitorum starts on the lateral epicondyle and sends four tendons across the back of the hand to fingers 2 to 5. It extends the fingers.
options: Correct. The four-tendon finger extensor is the extensor digitorum.
The extensor carpi ulnaris runs along the little-finger side to the fifth metacarpal; it moves the wrist, not the fingers.
The extensor carpi radialis longus runs along the thumb side to the second metacarpal and moves the wrist.
The flexor digitorum superficialis is on the palm side of the forearm.

why.correct: The supraspinatus tendon runs over the top of the shoulder joint, under the acromion, to the greater tubercle. Age-related wear, added to by years of overhead work, makes it the cuff tendon that tears most often. It helps abduct the arm, so a tear makes raising the arm to the side weak and painful.
options: The subscapularis runs across the front of the joint to the lesser tubercle, not under the acromion.
The short head of the biceps brachii starts on the coracoid process at the front and does not pass between the humerus and the acromion.
The teres major runs from the inferior angle of the scapula to the front of the humerus, well below the acromion.
Correct. The supraspinatus is the cuff tendon that tears most often.

why.correct: The rotator cuff is SITS: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis. Their tendons wrap the shoulder joint and hold the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity.
options: Yes. The S of SITS; it passes over the top of the joint.
Yes. The I of SITS; it lies below the spine of the scapula.
No. The teres major moves the humerus with the latissimus dorsi, but it does not join the cuff around the joint capsule.
Yes. The T of SITS; it lies along the lateral border of the scapula.
Yes. The final S of SITS, on the front of the scapula.
No. The deltoid lies over the cuff and abducts the arm, but it is not part of the cuff.

why.correct: The subscapularis runs from the front of the scapula across the front of the joint to the lesser tubercle. It rotates the arm medially.
options: The supraspinatus inserts on the greater tubercle.
Correct. Only the subscapularis uses the lesser tubercle.
The infraspinatus inserts on the greater tubercle.
The teres minor inserts on the greater tubercle.

why.correct: The serratus anterior pulls the medial border of the scapula forward around the chest wall and holds it flat against the ribs. When it fails, pushing forces the border to lift off: a winged scapula.
options: The rhomboids pull the scapula back toward the spine. Losing them would not make the border lift off the ribs during a push.
The trapezius elevates, retracts and depresses the scapula; the classic winging on pushing points to the muscle that holds the scapula to the chest wall.
Correct. A winged scapula on pushing means the serratus anterior is not working.
The pectoralis major moves the humerus, not the scapula.

why.correct: The deltoid runs from the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula over the top of the shoulder to the deltoid tuberosity. Pulling from above the joint, it lifts the arm out to the side.
options: The pectoralis major flexes and adducts the arm, bringing it forward and across the chest.
The latissimus dorsi extends and adducts the arm, pulling it down and back.
Correct. The deltoid is the prime mover of abduction.
The teres major adducts and extends the arm with the latissimus dorsi.

why.correct: The latissimus dorsi extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm, pulling it down and back from its broad origin on the lower back and pelvis.
options: Correct. Extension, adduction and medial rotation are the latissimus dorsi's actions.
The deltoid's main job is abduction, raising the arm, which is the opposite of this pull.
The trapezius moves the scapula, not the humerus.
The supraspinatus helps abduct the arm, the opposite direction.

why.correct: The wrist and finger extensors on the back of the forearm straighten the wrist and fingers. Losing them makes the wrist drop and the fingers stay bent, while the elbow flexors are unaffected.

variables.name: Ability to hold the wrist straight with the palm facing down
variables.why: The wrist extensors (extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris) hold the wrist up against gravity. Without them the hand drops.

variables.name: Ability to straighten the fingers at the knuckles
variables.why: The extensor digitorum is the main muscle that straightens the fingers from the forearm, and it is paralyzed.

variables.name: Strength of bending the elbow
variables.why: The elbow flexors (biceps brachii, brachialis and brachioradialis) still work normally.

why.correct: The limb works as a chain, each group moving the bone beyond the one it sits on: trunk muscles position the scapula, trunk and scapular muscles move the humerus, arm muscles move the forearm, and forearm muscles move the fingers.
options: Trunk muscles first turn the scapula, a base for raising the arm overhead.
Muscles from the trunk and girdle then lift the humerus.
The arm muscle on the back of the humerus straightens the elbow.
Forearm muscles send tendons into the fingers to grip.

why.correct: Most flexors on the palm side of the forearm start from a common tendon on the medial epicondyle, and most extensors on the back from a common tendon on the lateral epicondyle.
options: The olecranon is where the triceps brachii inserts, not where forearm flexors start.
Correct. The flexors share an origin on the medial epicondyle.
The coracoid process anchors the short head of the biceps brachii, the pectoralis minor and the coracobrachialis.
The deltoid tuberosity is where the deltoid inserts.

why.correct: The biceps brachii inserts on the radial tuberosity, which is why it can supinate the forearm. The olecranon is the insertion of its antagonist, the triceps brachii.
options: Correct step. The long head starts on a small bump above the glenoid cavity.
Correct step. The long head's tendon runs in the intertubercular groove.
Correct step. The two heads join into one belly on the front of the arm.
This is the wrong step. It inserts on the radial tuberosity, not the olecranon.

why.correct: Turning the palm up is supination. The supinator wraps the upper radius and rolls it, and the biceps brachii, pulling on the radial tuberosity, is the strongest supinator when the elbow is bent.
options: The pronators turn the palm down, the opposite movement.
The brachioradialis mainly flexes the elbow and the flexor carpi ulnaris flexes the wrist; neither is a main supinator.
The triceps brachii extends the elbow and the extensor digitorum extends the fingers; neither turns the palm up.
Correct. Supination by the supinator and biceps brachii.

why.correct: Pain at the lateral epicondyle that rises when the wrist is extended against resistance points to the extensors' common origin: tennis elbow.
options: Correct. The wrist extensors start from the lateral epicondyle, the outer bump.
The flexors start on the medial epicondyle, the inner bump; strain there is golfer's elbow.
The triceps brachii inserts on the olecranon, the point of the elbow, and extends the elbow rather than the wrist.
The rotator cuff is at the shoulder, not the elbow.

why.correct: The ulna stays put when the forearm pronates and supinates, so the brachialis always pulls in the same line. The radius rolls over the ulna; with the palm down, the biceps tendon is wrapped around the radius and its pull partly goes into turning the palm up rather than bending the elbow.
options: Neither muscle is circular; circular muscles surround openings. The difference comes from where each inserts.
Correct. Insertion on the non-rotating ulna versus the rolling radius explains it.
It is the other way round: the biceps brachii crosses the shoulder, and the brachialis starts on the humerus.
The biceps brachii still contracts with the palm down; it is simply less effective at flexing in that position.

why.correct: The thenar eminence is the mound at the base of the thumb, made of intrinsic hand muscles that abduct, flex and oppose the thumb.
options: Correct. The thenar eminence moves the thumb.
The medial epicondyle is a bone marking at the elbow, the origin of the forearm flexors.
The mound on the little-finger side is the hypothenar eminence.
The band at the wrist is the flexor retinaculum, which roofs the carpal tunnel.

why.correct: The rectus femoris runs straight down the middle of the front of the thigh from the ilium to the quadriceps tendon. It is the only part of the quadriceps femoris that crosses the hip.
options: The vastus intermedius lies deep, hidden under the rectus femoris.
The sartorius crosses the thigh diagonally, from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial tibia.
Correct. The straight middle muscle is the rectus femoris.
The vastus lateralis is on the outer side of the thigh.

why.correct: The sartorius runs diagonally from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial surface of the upper tibia. It is the longest muscle in the body.
options: Correct. The diagonal strap is the sartorius.
The gracilis is a thin strap too, but it runs straight down the inner thigh from the pubis.
The adductor longus is a short triangular muscle high on the inner thigh.
The tensor fasciae latae is a short muscle on the outer front of the hip.

why.correct: The gracilis (slender) runs from the lower pubis straight down the inner thigh to the medial surface of the upper tibia. It adducts the thigh and flexes the knee.
options: The sartorius runs diagonally across the front of the thigh, not straight down the inner edge.
The semitendinosus is on the back of the thigh, starting on the ischial tuberosity.
The adductor magnus is a large, deep muscle inserting along the femur, not a thin strap reaching the tibia.
Correct. The slender inner-thigh strap is the gracilis.

why.correct: The biceps femoris is the lateral hamstring. Its long head starts on the ischial tuberosity and its short head on the linea aspera; it inserts on the head of the fibula.
options: The semimembranosus is a medial hamstring.
Correct. The lateral hamstring is the biceps femoris.
The semitendinosus is a medial hamstring, with a long cord-like tendon.
The vastus lateralis is on the outer front of the thigh, part of the quadriceps femoris.

why.correct: The piriformis runs from the front of the sacrum to the greater trochanter and rotates the thigh laterally. A large nerve leaves the pelvis just below it.
options: The gluteus minimus lies higher on the outer ilium, fanning down to the front of the greater trochanter.
The quadratus lumborum is in the back wall of the abdomen, between the iliac crest and the twelfth rib.
Correct. This is the piriformis.
The iliacus lines the inner bowl of the ilium, on the front of the pelvis.

why.correct: The tibialis anterior lies along the lateral surface of the tibia and inserts on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal. It dorsiflexes and inverts the foot.
options: Correct. The muscle beside the shin is the tibialis anterior.
The fibularis longus is on the lateral side of the leg, over the fibula.
The extensor digitorum longus lies lateral to the tibialis anterior and runs to the toes.
The soleus is on the back of the leg, under the gastrocnemius.

why.correct: The soleus lies under the gastrocnemius, from the head of the fibula and back of the tibia to the calcaneal tendon. It crosses only the ankle and plantar flexes the foot.
options: The gastrocnemius is the two-headed superficial calf muscle that lies over it.
The tibialis posterior is the deepest muscle of the back of the leg.
Correct. The broad muscle under the gastrocnemius is the soleus.
The biceps femoris is a hamstring on the back of the thigh.

why.correct: The fibularis longus runs from the head and upper fibula; its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus and under the sole. It everts the foot.
options: The tibialis anterior lies on the front of the leg, beside the tibia.
Correct. The muscle over the fibula is the fibularis longus.
The extensor digitorum longus lies on the front of the leg and runs to the toes.
The gastrocnemius is the calf muscle on the back of the leg.

why.correct: The psoas major starts on the lumbar vertebrae and joins the iliacus to insert on the lesser trochanter. Together they form the iliopsoas, the prime mover of hip flexion.
options: The iliacus starts in the iliac fossa, the bowl of the ilium, not on the vertebrae.
The quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest up to the twelfth rib and does not cross the hip.
Correct. The muscle from the lumbar spine is the psoas major.
The pectineus is a short muscle from the pubis to just below the lesser trochanter.

why.correct: Bleeding and swelling inside the anterior compartment, wrapped in deep fascia that cannot stretch, raise the pressure until blood cannot flow through the capillaries. Pain out of proportion to the injury, and pain when the compartment's muscles are passively stretched (pointing the toes stretches the dorsiflexors), are the early signs. A pulse is often still present.
options: Correct. This is compartment syndrome of the front of the leg.
A calcaneal tendon rupture causes weakness rising onto the toes and pain at the back of the ankle, not severe pain in the front of the leg.
The hamstrings are on the back of the thigh, not the front of the leg.

Pain far worse than expected, and worse when the compartment's muscles are stretched, is not normal. A present pulse does not rule compartment syndrome out: the pressure in the large artery is far higher than the pressure in the compartment, so the pulse is often felt until late.

why.correct: The quadriceps femoris is four muscles: the rectus femoris and the vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius. All four insert through the quadriceps tendon, patella and patellar ligament on the tibial tuberosity.
options: Yes. The rectus femoris is the one part that crosses the hip.
Yes. The vastus lateralis is on the outer thigh.
No. The sartorius is also in the front of the thigh, but it inserts on the medial tibia and is not part of the quadriceps.
Yes. The vastus medialis is on the inner thigh above the knee.
Yes. The vastus intermedius lies deep under the rectus femoris.
No. The biceps femoris is a hamstring, on the back of the thigh.

why.correct: Standing on the right leg, the body's weight hangs to the left of the right hip. The right gluteus medius and minimus, abductors of the standing leg, pull the ilium down toward the greater trochanter and hold the pelvis level. When they are weak, the opposite side drops: a positive Trendelenburg sign.
options: The gluteus maximus mainly extends the hip, and the muscle that levels the pelvis belongs to the standing leg, here the right.
Correct. The standing leg's gluteus medius holds the pelvis level.
The iliopsoas flexes the hip; it does not hold the pelvis level in standing.
The adductor longus adducts the thigh and belongs to the lifted leg; it cannot hold up the pelvis on this side.

why.correct: An infant's thigh muscles are well developed while the gluteal and deltoid muscles are still small, so the middle third of the vastus lateralis on the outer thigh is the preferred site.
options: The deltoid is the usual vaccine site in adults, but in young infants it is too small.
The dorsogluteal site is avoided at every age: a large nerve lies close by and the fat layer is thick.
Correct. The vastus lateralis is preferred in infants.
The calf is not a standard injection site.

why.correct: The heel of the hand rests on the greater trochanter, the index finger on the anterior superior iliac spine and the middle finger spreads back along the iliac crest. The needle goes into the center of the V between the fingers, into the gluteus medius and minimus.
options: Correct. The heel of the hand goes on the greater trochanter.
The index finger, not the heel of the hand, goes on the anterior superior iliac spine.
The ischial tuberosity is the bone you sit on, far below the site.
The middle finger points back along the iliac crest; the heel of the hand is lower, on the femur.

why.correct: The gastrocnemius and soleus pull on the calcaneus only through the calcaneal tendon. With it ruptured, plantar flexion is weak and rising onto the toes fails, while the dorsiflexors on the front of the leg work normally.

variables.name: Ability to rise onto the toes of the right foot
variables.why: Rising onto the toes needs the gastrocnemius and soleus to pull the calcaneus up, and their shared tendon no longer connects them to it.

variables.name: Strength of pointing the right foot downward (plantar flexion)
variables.why: The main plantar flexors act through the calcaneal tendon. Only smaller muscles such as the tibialis posterior and the fibularis muscles are left to help.

variables.name: Strength of lifting the right toes toward the shin (dorsiflexion)
variables.why: Dorsiflexion is done by the tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus on the front of the leg, which are unaffected.

why.correct: The four muscles join the quadriceps tendon, which wraps the patella; below the patella it continues as the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.
options: The four parts of the quadriceps femoris generate the pull.
They converge on the shared quadriceps tendon above the knee.
The patella is a sesamoid bone within the tendon.
Below the patella, the band is called the patellar ligament.
It inserts on the tibial tuberosity, below the knee.

why.correct: The medial border of the femoral triangle is the adductor longus, the most anterior of the adductors.
options: The gracilis lies farther medially along the inner thigh; it does not form a border of the triangle.
Correct. The adductor longus forms the medial border.
The rectus femoris runs down the middle of the thigh, lateral to the triangle.
The iliopsoas lies in the floor of the triangle, not along its medial border.

why.correct: The hamstrings insert behind the knee's axis, on the head of the fibula (biceps femoris) and the medial tibia (semitendinosus and semimembranosus). The tibial tuberosity, on the front of the tibia, is where the quadriceps femoris inserts.
options: Correct step. The ischial tuberosity is the hamstrings' shared origin.
Correct step. Running behind the hip, they extend it.
Correct step. Crossing behind the knee, they flex it.
This is the wrong step. They insert on the fibula and medial tibia, not the tibial tuberosity.

why.correct: The hamstrings extend the hip and flex the knee, so they are lengthened by the opposite movements: hip flexion and knee extension. Doing both at once, as at the end of a sprinter's forward leg swing, stretches them at both ends.
options: Hip extension and knee flexion are the hamstrings' own actions, which shorten them.
Knee flexion shortens the hamstrings at their lower end, relieving some of the stretch from hip flexion.
Hip extension shortens them at the upper end, relieving the stretch from a straight knee.
Correct. Hip flexed with the knee straight stretches them the most.

why.correct: The iliopsoas (psoas major plus iliacus) passes in front of the hip joint to the lesser trochanter and is the prime mover of hip flexion.
options: The gluteus maximus is the prime mover of hip extension, the opposite movement.
Correct. The iliopsoas flexes the hip.
The biceps femoris extends the hip and flexes the knee.
The gluteus medius abducts the thigh and holds the pelvis level.

why.correct: The fibularis longus and brevis, in the lateral group of the leg, pass behind the lateral malleolus to the foot and turn the sole outward.
options: Both tibialis muscles invert the foot, turning the sole inward.
The gastrocnemius and soleus plantar flex the foot through the calcaneal tendon.
Correct. The fibularis muscles evert the foot.
The extensor digitorum longus mainly extends the toes, and the sartorius acts at the hip and knee, not the foot.

why.correct: The body's largest nerve runs out of the pelvis below the piriformis, close to this site, and a thick layer of fat over the gluteus maximus means the needle may not reach muscle. The ventrogluteal site avoids both problems.
options: The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the body; thickness is not the problem.
It has landmarks (the posterior superior iliac spine and greater trochanter), but they are harder to use, and the nearby nerve is the main risk.
Faster absorption would not be a reason to avoid it; the risks are the nerve and the fat.
Correct. A nearby large nerve and thick fat make it risky.

why.correct: The adductors and gracilis sit together in the medial compartment of the thigh and share one main action: adducting the thigh.
options: The anterior compartment of the thigh holds the quadriceps femoris and sartorius, which extend the knee.
Correct. The adductors form the medial compartment.
The posterior compartment of the thigh holds the hamstrings.
The lateral compartment of the leg holds the fibularis muscles, below the knee.

why.correct: The popliteal fossa is a diamond. The hamstring tendons form its upper borders (biceps femoris laterally, semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially), and the medial and lateral heads of the gastrocnemius form its lower borders.
options: The hamstring tendons form the upper borders, not the lower ones.
Correct. The two heads of the gastrocnemius form the lower borders.
The soleus and tibialis posterior lie deeper and lower in the calf, below the fossa.
The patella and patellar ligament are on the front of the knee.
